office.title: Indiana School Board Member
office.summary: A school board is the elected or appointed governing body of a public school corporation, the legal unit that runs a local school district [1, 2]. The board hires and evaluates the superintendent, adopts policies, and approves the annual budget, while the superintendent and staff run schools day to day [3]. Most boards have five or seven members serving staggered four-year terms [3]. Starting in 2026, candidates may list a political party, run as independents, or list no affiliation on the ballot, and there is no primary for these seats [2, 4].

facts.label: Term
facts.value: 4 years, with elections staggered so part of the board is chosen every two years [3]

facts.label: Elected
facts.value: At the November general election (November 3, 2026, or November 2028 for some seats); depending on the local organization plan, members represent the whole school corporation (at large) or a district within it, and some boards are wholly or partly appointed [2]

facts.label: Ballot label
facts.value: Each candidate chooses a party label, 'Independent', or no affiliation, shown next to the name; no primary and no straight-ticket voting for these races [2, 4]

facts.label: Pay
facts.value: Set by board resolution: an annual amount of no more than 10% of the lowest starting teacher salary in the school corporation, plus a capped per diem [5]

duties: Hires, evaluates and can dismiss the superintendent, and approves the hiring and firing of principals, teachers and other staff recommended by the superintendent [1, 7, 3].
Adopts the annual budget, appropriates funds and oversees school finances [1, 3].

Decides whether to ask voters to approve an operating referendum (an extra property tax levy); the board adopts the resolution and the Department of Local Government Finance reviews the ballot language for compliance with state law [8].
Approves contracts, buys and sells property, and decides on construction, repair and demolition of school buildings [1].

Bargains with the teachers' union over salary, wages and wage-related benefits such as health insurance and retirement; state law excludes teacher evaluation procedures from those bargaining subjects [9].
Writes and updates policies and rules for schools, often in a policy handbook, including the student handbook [1, 3].
Buys curricular materials, provides them to students without charge, and runs programs such as student transportation and school lunch [1].

Must adopt a process for parents and residents to ask that library material be removed as obscene or harmful to minors, review requests at public meetings and keep a public catalog of library materials [10].
Hears written appeals of student expulsions, unless the board has voted not to hear them [11].
Must take official action openly; Indiana's Open Door Law says public agencies' official action is to be conducted openly so the people may be fully informed [12, 13].

A school board member must have lived in the school corporation (and, for a district seat, the district) for at least one year before the election, and a teacher or other employee of the school corporation may not serve on its board [2].

What the board does not control: the State Board of Education adopts statewide academic standards [14], the General Assembly sets the state school funding formula in the state budget [15], and voucher (Choice Scholarship) eligibility is set by state law [16].
recent_changes: 2025: Senate Enrolled Act 287 allowed school board candidates to declare a party affiliation; the Indiana School Boards Association opposed the change, and a supporter quoted by WNDU, a Noblesville school board member, said it adds transparency [17].

2026: Candidates choose a party, 'Independent' or no affiliation on their nominating petition, and that choice appears on the ballot; a candidate claiming the Democratic or Republican party must have voted in that party's primary in the two most recent primaries they voted in, or have certification from the county party chair, or can be challenged and removed from the ballot [2].

July 2026: Chalkbeat reported, citing Indiana School Boards Association data, that 524 of 1,044 candidates chose a party, about 72% of them Republicans [18]; the Indiana Election Division's 2026 guidance and the wording of the law differ on the primary-voting test, a question county election boards decide [19].

February 2026: Senate Enrolled Act 25 set the order of school board candidates on the ballot, grouped by party, with candidates who list no affiliation placed after the party and independent candidates [20].

2025: Senate Enrolled Act 1, a property tax law, limits how much operating revenue districts can raise through taxes and restricts school referendums to statewide general elections in even-numbered years [21, 22].
2025: The same law requires districts to share operating revenue with brick-and-mortar charter schools that enroll their students, statewide starting in 2028 [21, 22].
2025: The state budget opened Choice Scholarship vouchers to all Indiana families starting in June 2026 [16].
2026: The Indianapolis Public Education Corporation, rather than the Indianapolis Public Schools board, now certifies Indianapolis Public Schools referendum questions for the ballot [20].

2023: Senate Enrolled Act 391 changed the so-called $1 law so the Indiana Department of Education can order districts that lost at least 10% of enrollment over five years to close schools under 60% capacity and offer them to charter schools [23].
2023: House Enrolled Act 1447 required school districts to set up procedures for complaints that library material is obscene or harmful to minors [10].

race_context: The district: the Metropolitan School District of Bluffton-Harrison serves Bluffton and Harrison Township in Wells County. It runs Bluffton-Harrison Elementary (pre-K through grade 4), Bluffton-Harrison Middle School (grades 5-8) and Bluffton High School [24, 25]. State enrollment counts rose from 1,632 students in 2018-19 to 1,782 in 2023-24, 1,813 in 2024-25 and 1,860 in 2025-26 [26]. Superintendent Brad Yates reported a K-12 average daily membership of 1,784.37 in August 2026 [27].

The board has five members: Julie Thompson (president), Mike Murray (vice president), Angie Sheets (secretary), Trent White and Tim Drayer [28, 29]. Three members are elected from Districts 1-3 and two at large, in staggered four-year terms [30, 31, 32, 33, 34].

Seats on the 2026 ballot: District 2 and one at-large seat, one member each, matching the state list [6]. The District 2 seat was won in 2022 by Bruce Holland [32]. He resigned in June 2024 after moving, and the board moved at-large member Angie Sheets, who lives in District 2, into the seat [35, 34]. Sheets is not on the 2026 ballot, so Mark Cobb is unopposed for the open seat [6]. The at-large seat is held by board president Julie Thompson, who is seeking a third term against Ryan Schisler [30, 32, 36, 6].

Earlier vacancies: Preston Kaehr, appointed to the other at-large seat in July 2024, won it in November 2024 and resigned in August 2025 [37, 33, 38]. Both Mark Cobb and Ryan Schisler applied for that vacancy and spoke to the board about their qualifications on Sept. 8, 2025. The board then appointed Tim Drayer to the seat through Dec. 31, 2028 [39].

Budget and SEA 1: the News-Banner reported on the district's plans after SB 1 (June 2025) and on expected further budget cuts in 2028 (April 2025) [40, 41]. In June 2026 the board chose Veregy for a guaranteed energy savings contract for solar power, and on Aug. 17, 2026 it unanimously approved the project's final scope for the middle and high schools [42, 27]. The News-Banner reported that the project should lower utility costs and help the district recover some of the operating money it lost to property-tax changes [43].

Safety referendum: in November 2023, Harrison Township voters rejected a school safety tax levy, 58% to 42%, a margin of 107 votes. It would have paid for two school resource officers and a mental health therapist; the district's three schools shared one officer at the time [25].

Staff pay: the board approved a teacher contract in October 2025. In July 2026 it approved one-time stipends paid in August: $750 for eligible teachers and other certified staff and $250 for eligible non-certified staff [44, 45].

Facilities and academics: in August 2026 the superintendent reported that high school paving and high school HVAC work were essentially finished and that the district was awaiting a cost estimate for structural repairs under the pool deck [27]. In 2025, 87.7% of the district's third graders passed IREAD [46]. The board discussed the state's proposed new accountability model in January 2026 [47]. In April 2026 Thompson reported that the board had been named an Indiana School Boards Association Level 1 Commendable Board for 2025 [48].

Forums: the News-Banner announced a candidate forum for some contested Wells County races on Monday, Oct. 5, 2026, and published a profile of the at-large race on Oct. 6 [49, 36]. Both articles are for subscribers only, and this guide could not read the candidates' statements in them.

candidates.summary: Incumbent and board president, first elected in 2018; listed as a Republican [28, 30, 6].
background: Chief administrative officer and chief nursing officer at Bluffton Regional Medical Center. She lives in Harrison Township, is 64, has served on the board of the Caylor Nickel Family YMCA and is board president of the Wells County Chamber of Commerce [36].

Won the at-large seat in 2018 (1,071 votes among five candidates) and again in 2022 (1,357 votes among three candidates) [30, 32]. Board secretary in 2025 and board president since January 2026; she also serves on the board's negotiations committee [50, 29].
path_to_ballot: Filed June 16, 2026, listed as a Republican [51, 6].
on_incumbent: Is a current board member. As president, she reported in April 2026 that the board had been named an ISBA Level 1 Commendable Board for 2025 [48]. She made the June 2026 motion choosing Veregy for the solar energy-savings contract [42].
gaps: The News-Banner's Oct. 6, 2026 profile of this race, and its forum coverage, are for subscribers only; this guide read only the opening lines and found no other statement of her plans.
No campaign website, questionnaire or endorsements found.
Not confirmed whether she reached the ballot by filing as a Republican or through a party nomination.

candidates.summary: Challenger for the at-large seat held by board president Julie Thompson; listed as nonpartisan [6].
background: Applied for the at-large board vacancy in 2025 and spoke at the board's Sept. 8, 2025 meeting about his background, qualifications and reasons for applying; the board appointed Tim Drayer [39].
Is listed in board minutes as an 'interested patron' at many meetings since then, including September and November 2025 and February, April, May, June and August 2026 [52, 53, 54, 48, 55, 42, 27].
gaps: This guide found no candidate website, social-media page, questionnaire or news interview for this candidate.
Occupation, community roles and ties to the schools are not reported in sources this guide could read. The minutes do not record what he said in September 2025.
The News-Banner's Oct. 6, 2026 profile of this race, and its forum coverage, are for subscribers only, so his stated positions could not be read.
No endorsements or campaign-finance reports found.

candidates.summary: Unopposed for the open District 2 seat; appointed incumbent Angie Sheets is not on the ballot [6, 34].
background: Applied for the at-large board vacancy in 2025 and spoke at the board's Sept. 8, 2025 meeting about his background, qualifications and reasons for applying; the board appointed Tim Drayer [39].
Is listed in board minutes as an 'interested patron' at meetings going back to June and July 2024, and at most meetings from September 2025 through August 2026 [34, 37, 52, 56, 29, 57, 58, 27].
path_to_ballot: Filed May 21, 2026, without a party; no one else filed for District 2 [51, 6].
gaps: This guide found no candidate website, social-media page, questionnaire or news interview for this candidate.
Occupation, community roles and ties to the schools are not reported in sources this guide could read. The minutes do not record what he said in September 2025.
No statements found on the budget, the solar project or other district issues.
No endorsements or campaign-finance reports found.
Other people named Mark Cobb appear in unrelated news from other states; nothing here refers to them.
